docs.title: Block Diagram
docs.text: Nikita Bangiyev, Team 201, Fill-A-Bot (automatic liquid dispenser)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I'm doing the main control board. It's the I2C host for the team. It reads the buttons, tells Clay's board to run the pump, gets the flow and weight readings from Cole's and Troy's boards, and shows the amount and status on a 16x2 LCD. My sensor is a photoresistor under the cup spot with an op amp, so the pump only starts when a cup is there.

Figure 1: Main control board block diagram (click to enlarge). Draw.io file: nikita-block-diagram.drawio

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
• 9V 2A regulated wall adapter (Triad WSU090-2000) into a barrel jack (Same Sky PJ-102AH)
  • LM1086IT-5.0 linear regulator makes 5V (1.5A max, 4.9 to 5.1V) for the whole board
  • The regulator has a heat sink (Same Sky HSE14-384225P) with an insulating pad, because its tab is at 5V
  • The Nano gets 5V on VTG with VOFF tied to GND
  • My power budget is 428mA with the 25% margin (see Power Budget)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• I switched from a 4-digit 7-segment display to a 16x2 LCD, because the team requirements need words like Ready, Filling, and Finished. The LCD has its own controller, so the HT16K33 driver is gone. It was discontinued anyway.
  • The op amp is needed because a photoresistor and resistor alone don't count as an analog sensor. U3A buffers the divider and U3B amplifies it with a gain of -3 around a 2.5V reference.
  • I switched from the LM7805 to the LM1086 because the LCD backlight needs 4.9 to 5.1V, and a 7805 can be 4.75 to 5.25V.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Everything on this page is for my individual subsystem, the Main Control Board.

My board reads the UP, DOWN, START, and STOP buttons, checks that a cup is there, runs the team I2C bus, and shows the amount and status on a display. Prices are from DigiKey for one part (October 2026).

docs.title: 1. Power Source
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Triad Magnetics WSU090-13009V 1.3A wall adapter$8.65/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive- In stock- Long 6 ft cord - Less than the regulator's 1.5A rating- Output can be off by 5%- Big body blocks the next outlet Option 2.MEAN WELL GST18U09-P1J9V 2A wall adapter$14.10/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 2A is more than enough- Lowest ripple- Wide temperature range - Most expensive- Out of stock- Short 1.2 m cord Option 3.Triad Magnetics WSU090-20009V 2A wall adapter$12.43/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 2A covers the regulator's full 1.5A- In stock- Long 6 ft cord - Costs more than the 1.3A one- Output can be off by 5%- Only rated up to 40 C

Choice: Option 3: Triad WSU090-2000

Rationale: The class power budget checks the adapter against the regulator's full 1.5A rating, so I need at least 1.5A. The 2A Triad passes that, it's in stock, and it costs less than the MEAN WELL. It has the 5.5 x 2.1 mm center-positive plug that fits my barrel jack.

docs.title: 2. 5V Linear Regulator
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Texas Instruments LM7805CT/NOPB5V 1.5A, TO-220$1.86/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Really common part- Built-in thermal protection- Easy to solder - Output can be 4.75 to 5.25V- About 2V dropout- Out of stock Option 2.STMicroelectronics L7805CV5V 1.5A, TO-220$1.08/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive- Lots in stock- Standard 7805 pinout - Output can be 4.75 to 5.25V- About 2V dropout- Gets just as hot as the others Option 3.Texas Instruments LM1086IT-5.0/NOPB5V 1.5A low dropout, TO-220$2.58/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Output stays 4.9 to 5.1V- Only 1.5V max dropout- In stock - Needs a 10uF tantalum output cap- Different pinout than a 7805- Costs a little more

Choice: Option 3: TI LM1086IT-5.0/NOPB

Rationale: My LCD backlight needs 4.9 to 5.1V, and the LM1086 is the only one that stays in that range. The 7805s can go up to 5.25V. It turns about 2W into heat at my full budget, so I'm adding a Same Sky HSE14-384225P heat sink with an insulating pad. That keeps it around 71 C, well under its 125 C limit.

docs.title: 3. Cup Sensor (Analog)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103Photoresistor (LDR)$0.72/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Big change between light and shadow- Sees normal room light- Used it in my photoresistor lab - Slow (about 60ms)- Room light changes the reading- Each one is a little different Option 2.Vishay TEPT4400Phototransistor$0.50/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive- Fast- Responds like the human eye - Big part-to-part difference- Can max out in bright light- Narrow viewing angle Option 3.Vishay BPW34Photodiode$1.37/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Very linear- Large sensing area- Fast - Needs a different amp circuit- Also picks up infrared- Really small currents

Choice: Option 1: Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103

Rationale: It's simple, inexpensive, and I already know how it works from lab. It sits under the cup spot with a 10k resistor, and a cup's shadow drops the voltage. A divider alone doesn't count as an analog sensor for this class, so it goes through the op amp below before the ADC. I'll still need to test it with our real cups, since a clear cup may not make much of a shadow.

docs.title: 4. Op Amp
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Microchip MCP6002-I/PDual op amp, 8-pin DIP$0.45/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rail-to-rail on 5V- Two op amps in one chip- Very low current - Higher offset- Only 1MHz- Doesn't quite reach the rails Option 2.Texas Instruments TLV2372IPDual op amp, 8-pin DIP$2.38/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rail-to-rail- Wide supply range- 3MHz - About 5x the price- Uses more current- Speed isn't needed Option 3.Texas Instruments OPA2340UADual op amp, SOIC-8$4.63/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Low offset- 5.5MHz- Rail-to-rail - Most expensive- Surface mount is harder to solder- Uses the most current

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6002-I/P

Rationale: A cup sensor is slow, so I don't need a fast op amp. The MCP6002 is inexpensive, comes in a DIP, and has two op amps. One buffers the LDR, and the other amplifies it with a gain of -3 around a 2.5V reference (Rin 10k, Rf 30k). I'll set the cup threshold in code after testing.

docs.title: 5. Display
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Lucky Light KW4-56NCUYA-P (Adafruit 811)4-digit 7-segment display$3.95/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Big, easy to read digits- Bright- Inexpensive - Can't show words like Ready or Filling- Can't show units- Needs a driver chip Option 2.Kingbright PDC54-11SURKWA2-character 14-segment display$5.60/each (need 4)DigiKey / Datasheet - Can show letters- Bright, high contrast- Big characters - 4 of them are too wide for my board- Needs a driver chip- Only 8 characters Option 3.Newhaven Display NHD-0216K1Z-FL-YBW16x2 character LCD$7.83/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Shows the amount, units, and status at once- Built-in controller, no driver chip- Backlit - Backlight uses up to 156mA- Needs a contrast pot- Uses 6 pins

Choice: Option 3: Newhaven NHD-0216K1Z-FL-YBW

Rationale: Our team requirements say the display has to show the amount, the units, and words like Ready, Filling, and Finished. The LCD is the only option that can do all of that at once. It wires straight to the Nano in 4-bit mode (RC0-RC5), so I don't need a driver chip or an I2C backpack.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This power budget checks that my 9V adapter and 5V regulator can run everything on my Main Control Board at the same time, with a 25% safety margin. It only covers my board, since each teammate has their own adapter and regulator. I used the class power budget template, and everything runs off one 5V rail.

docs.text: N/A. My board runs off a wall adapter.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The 2A adapter and the LM1086 can easily power everything on my board with the 25% margin, and nothing comes out negative. The biggest load is the LCD backlight. The regulator turns about 2W into heat, so it gets a heat sink, which keeps it around 71 C (its limit is 125 C).

Microchip only lists the PIC's max current at 3V, not 5V, so I used a safe upper estimate of 170mA for the Nano. The real number should be a lot lower, and I'll measure the actual board current once it's built.
